question: The persistence of chlordecone in the waters of Martinique and Guadeloupe has caused a major environmental and health crisis. This pollution is affecting not only the health of the local population, but also the biodiversity and economy of our outermost regions.

In this context, the study recently carried out by the Institute of Molecular Sciences of Marseille, published in February 2023 in the scientific journal ChemistrySelect, seems to offer promising prospects for more effective decontamination of these waters.

The research reported in this publication showed the effectiveness of hemicryptophanes, which are chemical compounds that are capable of ‘complexing’ and retaining the chlordecone molecule, offering a potential alternative to the activated carbon currently used in treatment plants. This scientific breakthrough raises important questions about the support given to such innovations in the regions concerned. 1.
What initiatives would the Commission envisage taking to facilitate the introduction and application in Martinique and Guadeloupe of this water decontamination technology using hemicryptophanes?
What funding and partnership mechanisms could be used to support the necessary further studies and accelerate the deployment of such solutions for tackling chlordecone pollution?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.5.2024) The Commission is aware of the presence of chlordecone in the waters in Martinique and Guadeloupe and the risks this poses to human health and the local biodiversity, as highlighted in the Strategy on the Outermost Regions1.

The Study on Living Conditions in the Outermost Regions2 also draws attention to the need to monitor the pollution and allocate resources to develop effective decontamination techniques in those regions. Chlordecone is prohibited in the EU since 2003.
Member States must take measures to ensure that water intended for human consumption is clean and meets minimum quality requirements set out in the recast Drinking Water Directive3.

The programmes 2014-2022 of Guadeloupe and Martinique under the European agricultural fund for rural development4 supported reducing the impact of chlordecone pollution through advice to farmers, investments to modernise holdings and cooperation for innovation and new agricultural practices.

Improving water quality and innovative technologies and tools for drinking water and wastewater treatment systems is among the priorities of the LIFE5 sub-programme on circular economy and quality of life.

Horizon Europe6 also funds research and innovation on solutions to address pollution and to guarantee clean and healthy water for all, notably through Cluster 6 (Food, Bioeconomy, Natural Resources, Agriculture and Environment)7 and the mission ‘A Soil Deal for Europe’8.

The European Regional Development Fund9 programmes in Guadeloupe and Martinique support projects to accelerate the deployment of solutions to tackle chlordecone pollution.
